storyboard.claim: Mrs. Green cannot act against James alone because the 1990s South physically, legally, and socially prevents her.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Law icon — the legal and social system restrains Mrs. Green alone, preventing her from acting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question posed in 159: why can't she destroy James herself?
storyboard.addedInformation: The chains make the constraint visible: she SEES the truth but cannot act on it.

storyboard.claim: A Black domestic worker cannot murder a wealthy white real estate investor without being destroyed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mrs. Green diminished beside James standing tall — the gulf in power between them.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Specifies the constraint from 160: here is why she is bound.
storyboard.addedInformation: Staging James looming over a slumped Mrs. Green makes the imbalance visceral without an icon.

storyboard.claim: The police would not investigate; they would imprison her or worse.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Law icon — the legal system that would destroy her, not protect her.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The specific mechanism of the power gap in 161: the law itself.
storyboard.addedInformation: Law reads as the legal system, which is exactly what threatens her here.

storyboard.claim: Mrs. Green needs Patricia's white privilege and social capital as a protective shield.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Shield icon — the narrator's own word; Patricia's privilege literally shields the plan.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After naming why Mrs. Green cannot act (law, power): here is what she needs instead.
storyboard.addedInformation: Patricia stands in front of Mrs. Green: the shield is a person, not an abstraction.

storyboard.claim: Mrs. Green survives within the infrastructure of exploitation by redirecting its resources against the predator.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mrs. Green pointing, directing — she is a tactician aiming the system's own weapons.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From needing a shield (163) to how she actually wields it: from within.
storyboard.addedInformation: The pointing action makes the directing literal; she orchestrates, she does not fight.

storyboard.claim: It is tactically brilliant — hacking the system from the inside.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mrs. Green thinking, strategizing — the narrator calls it hacking, she is the hacker.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The host's verdict on the strategy described in 164.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: restates 164 as summary; the think pose differentiates it from the previous pointing.

storyboard.claim: Patricia's escalating anger mirrors how female rage is policed in the real world.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia talking, straining to be heard — her anger is constrained by the system.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shifts from Mrs. Green's tactical constraint (165) to Patricia's emotional constraint.
storyboard.addedInformation: The callout names the sociological reality the narrator is mapping onto the plot.

storyboard.claim: Patricia goes to Grace's house desperate to convince her James is a monster.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia reaching toward Grace in the kitchen — desperate, pleading.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the abstract point about policed anger (166) to the specific scene where it breaks.
storyboard.addedInformation: The kitchen set anchors the confrontation in Grace's domestic space.

storyboard.claim: Grace is meticulously washing her grandmother's antique china — obsessive domestic ritual.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Grace holding a cup (china saucer) at the kitchen sink, focused on the fragile object.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Patricia reached for Grace (167); Grace is focused on china instead of listening.
storyboard.addedInformation: The cup in hand makes the domestic obsession tangible; her neutral face says she is ignoring Patricia.

storyboard.claim: Grace obsesses over cleaning etiquette while children in Six Mile are literally dying.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Grave icon — children are dying; the icon reads as death, which is the literal claim.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The same kitchen, same Grace, but the callout names what her china-washing costs.
storyboard.addedInformation: Grace's neutral idle face next to a grave makes the indifference obscene.

storyboard.claim: Patricia finally snaps, erupting and screaming at Grace.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia pointing at Grace, face twisted — she has broken through her own restraint.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The calm kitchen from 168-169 explodes; the reaching (167) becomes confrontation.
storyboard.addedInformation: Surprised expression reads as the volcanic moment of breaking, not curiosity.

storyboard.claim: Patricia shatters the polite southern facade right there in the kitchen.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mask icon — the facade is a false face; strike-through says it is being destroyed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The snap from 170 now names what it shatters: the mask of southern gentility.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike style makes the destruction visible: the facade is crossed out, not maintained.

storyboard.claim: To be heard, a woman must embrace the exact hysteria she is accused of; polite concern achieves nothing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia talking with a pained face — she must perform the very breakdown they expect.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The narrator pulls back from the kitchen scene (171) to name the systemic pattern.
storyboard.addedInformation: The sad expression says this is not triumph but a trap: she must lose dignity to be heard.

storyboard.claim: Handing over well-organized notes achieves nothing; Patricia must burn her own social standing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia holding the notes that failed her — the evidence nobody would accept.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the abstract principle (172) to the concrete cost: her own reputation.
storyboard.addedInformation: The notes in hand show what DID NOT work; the callout names what she must destroy instead.

storyboard.claim: Patricia must face a psychiatric hold arranged by her own husband.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Medical icon — Carter's psychiatric credentials weaponized; Patricia slumps, institutionalized by the man who should protect her.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The cost of screaming (173): her own husband locks her away.
storyboard.addedInformation: Carter as second cast makes the betrayal specific: her doctor-husband is the instrument.

storyboard.claim: To trap James, Patricia must offer herself as literal bait.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Target icon — Patricia makes herself the target; she stands exposed beside the predator.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the psychiatric hold (174) to the final extreme: she sacrifices her body.
storyboard.addedInformation: Target reads as being aimed at, which is precisely what bait is.

storyboard.claim: Patricia kneels before James in an empty house, letting him bite and feed on her blood.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia slumped (kneeling) before James in an empty room — the physical submission.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The bait from 175 in action: she is now being consumed.
storyboard.addedInformation: The slump makes the kneeling posture visible; the empty room set isolates them.

storyboard.claim: She feels her life slipping away just to keep him distracted long enough for the others to strike.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia alone, fading — her life draining is the price of the trap.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues 176: the feeding goes on, she endures.
storyboard.addedInformation: Removing James from view isolates Patricia's sacrifice; she is alone with her draining life.

storyboard.claim: Her physical subjugation is a weapon — the ultimate sacrifice of the self to destroy the abuser.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Shield icon — Patricia gives up her own protection, sacrificing her shield so the group can survive.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The thematic summary of 175-177: all that suffering was weaponized.
storyboard.addedInformation: The shield reads as protection; her slumped posture says she has surrendered it — the sacrifice IS giving up her shield.

storyboard.claim: She uses the fact that James views her as nothing more than a resource to trap him.
storyboard.concreteVisual: James standing idle, indifferent — he sees Patricia as a thing, not a threat.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reframes 176-178 from James's blind spot: he never saw her as dangerous.
storyboard.addedInformation: James as first cast with neutral expression shows his contemptuous indifference.

storyboard.claim: From the outside, Patricia claiming her neighbor is a vampire looks like she has lost her mind.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia on the suburban street, wild-eyed and talking — she looks unhinged to everyone around her.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The hosts step back from the sacrifice (179) to see how Patricia looks to outsiders.
storyboard.addedInformation: The street set returns to the suburb's perspective; surprised expression reads as frantic.

storyboard.claim: Patricia does not jump to vampires — she builds a rational, evidence-based case that her neighbors still dismiss.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An everyman neighbor pointing at Patricia — even her rational evidence is dismissed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends 180: the outside perspective now from a neighbor's eyes.
storyboard.addedInformation: Everyman as first cast puts the viewer in the neighbor's shoes, not Patricia's.

storyboard.claim: Patricia did not start with vampires; she built a meticulous, grounded, entirely secular case.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Magnifier icon — close forensic examination; Patricia holds her evidence notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The defense against 180-181: she was NOT raving; she was investigating.
storyboard.addedInformation: Magnifier reads as examination, which is exactly what a secular case is.

storyboard.claim: She gathered trackmarks, license plates, financial anomalies, missing persons — forensic evidence.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia pointing at the evidence items she compiled — a detective's board of concrete proof.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The specific contents of the secular case from 182.
storyboard.addedInformation: The callout names concrete physical evidence, not abstract suspicion.

storyboard.claim: She had the folder; the logical criminal truth was aggressively and violently rejected by the men in power.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia holding out her folder of evidence while Carter turns away — the rejection in the room.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The case from 182-183 hits the wall: Carter will not look at it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Carter as second cast identifies WHO rejects: her own husband, the man with authority.

storyboard.claim: She tried logic, evidence, law — the master's tools — and they refused to work for her.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Law icon — the legal system she tried to use; Patricia reaching for it but unable to grasp it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The summary of 182-184: the entire rational approach failed.
storyboard.addedInformation: The reach action makes visible that the tools are there but will not respond to her hand.

storyboard.claim: When human justice fails, her unhinged anger is the only force that can break the infrastructure protecting him.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia pointing furiously — her anger is the only remaining weapon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The master's tools failed (185); anger is the tool that replaces them.
storyboard.addedInformation: Surprised expression reads as explosive fury, not curiosity.

storyboard.claim: The grand finale completely inverts the domesticity trap that suffocated these women for centuries.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia talking, transitional — the host is setting up the climax.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pivots from anger (186) to the structural inversion of the ending.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: transitional beat; the callout does the work of teasing the finale.

storyboard.claim: This is NOT the classic horror finale where the final girl defeats the monster with a magical artifact or brute strength.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia standing idle — no weapon, no magic; the strike-through rejects the trope.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The inversion teased in 187: here is what the ending is NOT.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike crosses out the expected horror tool; Patricia's empty hands confirm its absence.

storyboard.claim: James Harris lies paralyzed on the floor; the women of the book club surround him.
storyboard.concreteVisual: James slumped on the floor, low angle — the predator is finally down.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After rejecting the classic trope (188): here is what actually happens.
storyboard.addedInformation: Low angle emphasizes James's fall; Patricia above him reverses the power dynamic.

storyboard.claim: They calmly slip on green gardening knee pads to protect their joints — no garlic, no holy water.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia and Grace calm and methodical, preparing — the mundane replacing the mythic.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From James on the floor (189) to what the women do: domestic preparation.
storyboard.addedInformation: The neutral expressions are the point: eerily calm, as if this is a gardening task.

storyboard.claim: They open a plastic cooler — the exact kind from a PTA picnic — but it holds saws and chain mail gloves.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The women beside the opened cooler — a domestic object turned slaughterhouse kit.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From knee pads (190) to the next domestic item repurposed: the escalation.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the cooler's horror contents are in the narration; the visual shows only the mundane container.

storyboard.claim: The master's tools CAN dismantle the master's house — if repurposed correctly.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow diagram: domestic tools -> repurposed -> dismantle the house. The structural thesis of the climax.
storyboard.onScreenText: DOMESTIC TOOLS -> REPURPOSED -> DISMANTLE THE HOUSE
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The conceptual summary of 190-191: the narrator names the pattern.
storyboard.addedInformation: The flow shows a causal chain the narrator only states as a conclusion.

storyboard.claim: The book club weaponizes their own oppression; they do not become martial arts experts.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia and Grace directing the operation — coordinated, purposeful, domestic.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The principle from the diagram (192) now named as the book's genius.
storyboard.addedInformation: Pointing action shows them directing: this is logistical coordination, not combat.

storyboard.claim: They use the exact domestic tools and logistical coordination that kept them trapped for decades.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Casserole icon — the book's central symbol of domestic labor, now repurposed as a weapon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the abstract principle (193) to the specific toolkit: domestic infrastructure.
storyboard.addedInformation: The casserole makes the domestic-labor-as-weapon thesis literal and book-specific.

storyboard.claim: They literally dismember the predator with chilling efficiency — like repurposing a factory line.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The women standing idle, calm — the eerie composure IS the horror.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The domestic tools from 194 in action: efficient, mechanical, cold.
storyboard.addedInformation: Neutral expressions on both women make the factory-line metaphor land without staging violence.

storyboard.claim: They chop, clean, and dispose with the same invisible efficiency they used for carpools and casseroles.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The women standing in a clean room — the cleanup is already done, nothing to see.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues 195: the efficiency extends to the cleanup, not just the act.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: builds on 195 without much new visual; the callout intensifies the tone.

storyboard.claim: The skills from maintaining the perfect suburb are the exact skills required for a perfect untraceable murder.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Casserole icon — the narrator literally names bereavement casseroles; the domestic network is the murder weapon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The payoff of 194-196: domestic labor = the perfect crime.
storyboard.addedInformation: The cup in hand says post-cleanup composure — they could be at a PTA meeting.

storyboard.claim: They monetize their own invisibility — no one suspects them because society believes they are incapable of violent action.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mask icon — their harmless-housewife image is a false face that hides what they did.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the act (195-197) to why they get away with it: the mask of domesticity.
storyboard.addedInformation: Walking on the street: they leave the scene and re-enter the suburb, invisible again.

storyboard.claim: Their erasure becomes their alibi — the system that silenced them now protects them.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Patricia standing alone, unremarkable — her ordinariness IS the alibi.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The final inversion of the mask from 198: the same invisibility that trapped them now saves them.
storyboard.addedInformation: Transitional beat; the calm idle after violence says the infrastructure has reset around them.
